nodes.name: The Blueprint - OSI & Data Movement
nodes.description: Learn OSI Model, Encapsulation, PDU, and MAC Addressing before testing

encounters.title: The Blueprint - How Data Moves
encounters.scenario:
A network technician is troubleshooting why a computer cannot reach a local printer. To find the problem, they must understand how data travels from an application through the physical wires.

Data does not move as one giant block; it is broken down through a process called ENCAPSULATION. As data moves down the OSI MODEL (a 7-layer framework used to understand network functions), each layer adds its own information.

At each layer, the data takes on a new form called a PROTOCOL DATA UNIT (PDU).
- At Layer 4 (Transport), the PDU is called a SEGMENT
- At Layer 3 (Network), the PDU is called a PACKET
- At Layer 2 (Data Link), the PDU is called a FRAME

To move these frames between devices on the same local network, we use a MAC ADDRESS (Media Access Control). This is a permanent, physical address burned into the network interface card (NIC) of every device.
encounters.question: What does PDU stand for, and what is the PDU called at Layer 2?
encounters.explanation: PDU stands for Protocol Data Unit. At Layer 2 (Data Link), the PDU is called a Frame. At Layer 3 it's a Packet, at Layer 4 it's a Segment.

encounters.title: OSI Layer Basics
encounters.scenario:
The OSI MODEL is a 7-layer framework that standardizes network functions:

Layer 7 - APPLICATION: User interfaces (browsers, email)
Layer 6 - PRESENTATION: Data formatting, encryption
Layer 5 - SESSION: Managing connections/dialogues
Layer 4 - TRANSPORT: TCP/UDP, reliable delivery
Layer 3 - NETWORK: IP addressing, routing between networks
Layer 2 - DATA LINK: MAC addressing, frames, local delivery
Layer 1 - PHYSICAL: Cables, signals, bits on the wire

Mnemonic: Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away
encounters.question: Which OSI layer uses IP addresses to route packets between different networks?
encounters.explanation: Layer 3 (Network Layer) handles IP addressing and routing between different networks. Layer 2 uses MAC addresses for local delivery only.

nodes.name: The Language of Transport - Protocols & Ports
nodes.description: Learn TCP/UDP, common protocols, and port numbers before testing

encounters.title: TCP vs UDP - The Transport Methods
encounters.scenario:
Computers communicate using protocols at Layer 4 (Transport). There are two primary methods:

TCP (TRANSMISSION CONTROL PROTOCOL) - Connection-oriented and reliable. It establishes a connection, sends data, and verifies delivery. Used for web browsing, file transfers.

UDP (USER DATAGRAM PROTOCOL) - Connectionless and fast. It sends data without verifying delivery. Used for streaming video, VoIP, DNS queries.

To keep traffic organized, services use PORT NUMBERS (like doors on a device):
- HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol): Web traffic, Port 80
- HTTPS: Secure web, Port 443
- DNS (Domain Name System): Name resolution, Port 53
- SSH (Secure Shell): Remote command line, Port 22
- SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol): Sending email, Port 25
- FTP (File Transfer Protocol): File transfers, Port 21
- RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol): Remote GUI, Port 3389
- SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol): Monitoring, Port 161
- LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol): Directory services, Port 389
- DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol): IP assignment, Ports 67/68
encounters.question: What does TCP stand for, and is it reliable or fast?
encounters.explanation: TCP stands for Transmission Control Protocol. It is connection-oriented and reliable - it verifies data delivery. UDP is the fast but unreliable alternative.

encounters.title: Common Protocols and Their Ports
encounters.scenario:
Study this reference table of common network protocols:

PROTOCOL        | PURPOSE                          | PORT
----------------|----------------------------------|------
HTTP            | Web browsing (unsecured)         | 80
HTTPS           | Web browsing (secured)           | 443
DNS             | Name to IP resolution            | 53
SSH             | Secure remote command line       | 22
SMTP            | Sending email                    | 25
FTP             | File transfers                   | 21
RDP             | Remote desktop GUI               | 3389
SNMP            | Network device monitoring        | 161
LDAP            | Directory services/auth          | 389
DHCP            | Automatic IP assignment          | 67/68
encounters.question: Which protocol and port is used for secure remote command-line access to a server?
encounters.explanation: SSH (Secure Shell) uses Port 22 for secure remote command-line access. Telnet is the unsecured alternative. RDP is for graphical remote desktop.

nodes.name: The Gatekeepers - Security & Traffic Flow
nodes.description: Learn IDS/IPS, UTM, Stateful firewalls, and traffic directions before testing

encounters.title: Security Systems - IDS vs IPS vs UTM
encounters.scenario:
Network security uses different types of monitoring systems:

IDS (INTRUSION DETECTION SYSTEM) - Monitors traffic and ALERTS when something suspicious is detected. It watches but does not block.

IPS (INTRUSION PREVENTION SYSTEM) - Monitors traffic and ACTIVELY BLOCKS threats. It can stop attacks in real-time.

UTM (UNIFIED THREAT MANAGEMENT) - An all-in-one security appliance combining firewall, IDS/IPS, antivirus, and other security functions into a single device.
encounters.question: What does IDS stand for, and does it alert or block?
options: Internal Data Scanner - Both alerts and blocks
encounters.explanation: IDS stands for Intrusion Detection System. It only ALERTS on suspicious activity. IPS (Intrusion Prevention System) is what actively blocks threats.

encounters.title: Firewall Types and Traffic Directions
encounters.scenario:
FIREWALL TYPES:

STATELESS FIREWALL - Examines each packet in isolation. Only checks source/destination addresses and ports. No memory of previous packets.

STATEFUL FIREWALL - Remembers the state of connections. If you sent a request out, it remembers and allows the response back in automatically. More intelligent than stateless.

TRAFFIC DIRECTIONS (Data Center Context):

NORTH-SOUTH TRAFFIC - Traffic moving in and out of the data center (client to server, external to internal). Traditional firewall focus.

EAST-WEST TRAFFIC - Traffic moving sideways between servers within the data center. Growing security concern as attacks spread internally.
encounters.question: What type of firewall remembers the state of connections and allows return traffic automatically?
encounters.explanation: A Stateful firewall remembers connection states and allows return traffic automatically. Stateless firewalls check each packet in isolation without memory.

nodes.name: The Virtual Frontier - Cloud & Virtualization
nodes.description: Learn IaaS/PaaS/SaaS, VPC, and NFV before testing

encounters.title: Cloud Service Models - IaaS, PaaS, SaaS
encounters.scenario:
Cloud computing has three service models based on how much the provider manages:

IAAS (INFRASTRUCTURE AS A SERVICE) - You rent raw hardware (servers, storage, networking). You manage the operating system and applications. Example: AWS EC2, Azure VMs.

PAAS (PLATFORM AS A SERVICE) - You only manage your code/applications. The provider manages the hardware AND the operating system. Example: Google App Engine, Heroku.

SAAS (SOFTWARE AS A SERVICE) - You just use the software via a browser or app. The provider manages everything. Example: Microsoft 365, Gmail, Dropbox.
encounters.question: What does IaaS stand for, and what do you manage in this model?
options: Infrastructure as a Service - You manage OS and applications
Internet as a Service - Provider manages everything
Internal Application Service - You manage hardware only
Integrated Access System - You manage nothing
encounters.explanation: IaaS = Infrastructure as a Service. You rent the hardware but manage the operating system and applications yourself. PaaS = Platform as a Service (you manage apps only). SaaS = Software as a Service (you just use the software).

encounters.title: VPC and NFV - Virtual Cloud Concepts
encounters.scenario:
VPC (VIRTUAL PRIVATE CLOUD) - A private, isolated section of a public cloud where you can launch resources in a virtual network that you define. Your VPC is logically isolated from other VPCs.

NFV (NETWORK FUNCTIONS VIRTUALIZATION) - Replacing physical network hardware (like routers, firewalls, load balancers) with software running on virtual machines. This makes networks more flexible and scalable.
encounters.question: What does VPC stand for?
encounters.explanation: VPC = Virtual Private Cloud. It's your private, isolated slice of a public cloud provider's infrastructure.

nodes.name: The Physical Layer - Fiber & Transceivers
nodes.description: Learn SMF/MMF and SFP before testing fiber questions

encounters.title: Fiber Types - SMF vs MMF
encounters.scenario:
FIBER OPTIC CABLING TYPES:

SMF (SINGLE-MODE FIBER) - Uses a tiny core (8-10 microns) and a laser light source. Can transmit data over very long distances (miles/kilometers). Used for campus backbones, WAN connections.

MMF (MULTI-MODE FIBER) - Uses a larger core (50-62.5 microns) and LED light sources. Limited to shorter distances (up to 550m typically). Used within buildings, data centers.

The difference: Single-mode = long distance. Multi-mode = short distance but cheaper transceivers.
encounters.question: What does SMF stand for, and what is its primary advantage?
encounters.explanation: SMF = Single-Mode Fiber. Its primary advantage is the ability to transmit over very long distances using laser light and a small core.

encounters.title: SFP - The Hot-Swappable Transceiver
encounters.scenario:
SFP (SMALL FORM-FACTOR PLUGGABLE) - A compact, hot-swappable transceiver module that plugs into a switch port. It converts the electrical signals from the switch into the light signals needed for fiber optic cables.

SFP modules allow you to:
- Connect different cable types (copper or fiber)
- Support different speeds (1G, 10G)
- Swap without powering down the switch (hot-swappable)

Without an SFP module, you cannot connect fiber directly to a standard copper Ethernet switch port.
encounters.question: What does SFP stand for?
encounters.explanation: SFP = Small Form-factor Pluggable. It's the hot-swappable module that connects fiber cables to switch ports.
